summary: Describes problems that arise when a device is connected to several networks at once and receives configuration from each. Some settings apply to the whole device and others to one interface, so conflicts can cause traffic to use the wrong interface or names to clash. It is a problem statement, not a solution.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine getting different directions from two friends at the same time. A phone on wifi and mobile data can get mixed-up instructions, and this document lists the troubles that causes.

questions: why does my device pick the wrong network interface
why does my device pick the wrong network
subtitle: When a device has multiple networks, configuration gets conflicted

tldr.problem: Devices with multiple network interfaces (mobile phones, laptops with WiFi and cellular, VPN) receive configuration from each network. Some settings apply to the whole device, and conflicting settings cause traffic to use the wrong interface or names to resolve incorrectly.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC lists the problems: DNS failures when private domains are reachable on only one interface, routing conflicts when the same destination is reachable via different paths, and policy conflicts when networks send incompatible rules.
tldr.outcome: No single solution is proposed; the RFC defines the scope and underlying causes so that future work can address these issues systematically. It is a problem statement, not a solution.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Devices with multiple interfaces or single interfaces on multiple domains

today: RFC 6418 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains the foundational problem statement for multihoming research in the IETF. Its issues motivated the MIPSHOP, SHIM6, MPTCP and other working groups addressing multihoming scenarios.

sections.title: Multiple Networks, One Device
sections.content:
Modern devices are often connected to multiple networks at the same time. A laptop might use both Ethernet and WiFi. A smartphone uses WiFi, 4G, and VPN. Each network connection is a provisioning domain: a set of configuration information (like DNS servers, default gateway, address prefixes) and the interface attached to it.

The core problem is that some configuration is interface-specific (IP address, link prefix), while other configuration is considered global to the device (DNS servers, default route, address selection policy). When different networks send conflicting global configuration, the device must choose which to use, and choosing wrong means broken connectivity or security problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone gets instructions from WiFi and from mobile data. Some instructions are just for that connection, but others are device-wide. If it picks the wrong global instruction, the phone breaks.

sections.title: DNS and Naming Problems
sections.content:
The most common issue is DNS. Consider a device (M1) with one interface on a corporate network (I1) and another on the public Internet (I2). The corporate network DNS server (S1) knows private names like 'a.private.example.com'. The public DNS server (S2) serves the Internet.

Several failures occur: (1) The device might route queries to S1 through I2, missing the server entirely. (2) The device might keep only one DNS server address and query S2, which returns NXDOMAIN for the private name. (3) S2 might resolve the private name to a different IP than S1 would, sending traffic to the wrong server. (4) Both networks might use private address space with overlapping ranges, so an IP address resolved on one network is unreachable on another.

DNS64 synthesized addresses are guaranteed valid only on the network where learned; using them elsewhere loses traffic. Captive portals that redirect DNS can prevent legitimate access until the user authenticates, creating a catch-22.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone asks WiFi's DNS server a question, but WiFi says 'never heard of it,' even though the company's WiFi actually knows the answer.

sections.title: Routing and Interface Selection
sections.content:
When a device wants to reach an IP address, it looks up a route. With multiple interfaces, the route table might send traffic through the wrong interface. Problems include: (1) Only one default route is known, and the destination is only reachable through the other interface. (2) Multiple default routes exist but the device chooses the less desirable path (worse latency, higher cost, lower bandwidth). (3) A specific route learned from one network conflicts with a default route from another, causing traffic to use the wrong interface.

The device also must choose a source address. Some addresses are valid only on certain interfaces; using an invalid source address gets packets filtered by source address filters along the path, and replies never return.

There is no standard method for the device to know which interface is best. Different network operators push conflicting routing policies (like ANDSF in 3GPP). The device has no way to merge or reconcile them.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone has two routes to the same place: a fast WiFi route and a slow mobile route. Your phone picks the slow one by accident.

sections.title: Policy Conflicts and Configuration
sections.content:
Modern networks distribute policies to devices, not just IP addresses. Networks send address selection policies (which source addresses to prefer), routing policies (which destinations to send through which interface), and access selection policies (which networks to use when). When multiple provisioning domains send conflicting policies, the device must merge them.

Merging can break connectivity: (1) A device might choose a source address from one network that is not reachable from the network packets are sent through. (2) Each provisioning domain pushes routing policies, and the device has no way to determine priority or merge them. (3) Local user policy (like 'prefer WiFi') might conflict with network policy (like 'overloaded access networks'), and the device does not know which to obey.

Configuration conflicts also occur when a single interface is attached to multiple provisioning domains through techniques like dual-stack or VPN. Even with one interface, a device may need multiple DNS servers, multiple default gateways, and multiple source addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: WiFi says 'use this address,' and mobile says 'no, use that one.' Your phone sends packets from the wrong address, and the answer never comes back.

sections.title: Session Management and Mobility
sections.content:
When a new, better interface becomes available (like switching to WiFi when mobile data was in use), the device must decide: move existing sessions to the new interface or keep them on the old one and start new sessions on the new interface? If the session switches interfaces, the TCP connection breaks unless mobility protocols like Mobile IPv6 are used. If the device chooses a new interface, it must also handle IP connectivity checks: some interfaces appear to have IP connectivity but cannot reach any real content (like a captive portal on an open WiFi).

For single-interface devices on multiple provisioning domains, the device must choose which provisioning domain is active for each application or connection, and manage the selection policy. This requires awareness of which services are reachable through which domain, which is not automatically available to applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone connected to WiFi but the WiFi doesn't actually work (you haven't logged into the captive portal yet). Your phone should have checked before switching.
